subject.title: Oakland — Measure FF (Transfer Tax on Foreclosures)

text: Shall the measure amending Oakland’s Real Property Transfer Tax Ordinance to eliminate the foreclosure exception for all property transfers except transfers converting commercial property to certain housing or healthcare uses, transfers to community banking organizations, and certain transfers of residential properties of four units or less, and allowing the City Council to establish, amend, or remove foreclosure-related exceptions, raising approximately $4-$13 million annually pursuant to tax rates in Oakland Municipal Code section 4.20.020, beginning January 1, 2027 until repealed, be adopted?

Oakland’s Real Property Transfer Tax (Oakland Municipal Code Chapter 4.20) imposes a tax on certain transfers of real property in the City of Oakland assessed as a percentage of the value of the transfer. Currently, the Real Property Transfer Tax generally exempts transfers made pursuant to foreclosure proceedings and transfers in lieu of foreclosure, meaning such transfers are not subject to the tax. This Measure would amend the City’s Real Property Transfer Tax to eliminate the general exception for foreclosure-related transfers, and would only allow foreclosure-related exceptions for transfers converting commercial property to certain housing or healthcare uses, transfers to community banking organizations, and transfers of properties that consist of four residential units or less to a natural person or family trust. The Measure would also allow the City Council to, by ordinance, amend and/or remove those remaining foreclosure-related exceptions, and establish other foreclosure-related exceptions.
The Measure specifies that the property value for purposes of taxing foreclosure-related transfers would be the fair market value of the interest or property conveyed, not excluding the value of any lien or encumbrance remaining at the time of transfer, or the fair market value of the real property that experienced a change in control and ownership. Foreclosure-related transfers that did not qualify for an exception would be taxed at the rates that are already set in Oakland Municipal Code Section 4.20.020. Any additional revenue generated by this Measure would be general purpose funding that the City may use for any municipal purpose. This Measure would not impose a transfer tax on any entity or transfer if such taxation was otherwise prohibited by state or federal law.
This Measure was placed on the ballot by the City Council. This Measure will take effect on January 1, 2027, only if a majority (greater than 50%) of voters voting on the Measure vote “Yes.”

When families buy homes, they pay Oakland’s real property transfer tax. But when hedge funds or investors acquire property through foreclosure or deed-in-lieu transfers they are exempt, avoiding a tax even for buildings worth tens of millions of dollars.
In just the first half of 2026, this loophole has cost Oakland up to $25 million. That’s less for paving roads, responding faster to 911 calls, and stopping illegal dumping. Today’s tax code subsidizes a “loan-to-own” strategy that sophisticated investors increasingly take advantage of. They buy real-estate debt at a discount then use that to acquire property tax-free. Oaklanders make up the difference through service cuts and other taxes.
Measure FF closes this loophole so foreclosure transfers are taxed fairly. It exempts homeowners in foreclosure. It also exempts regular homebuyers, giving them a leg up on speculators like BlackRock who have to pay. Fifteen states already tax foreclosure transfers, and Mayor Daniel Lurie is bringing a similar measure to San Francisco this election. Oakland can’t let this money walk out the door. Measure FF makes Oakland’s budget more resilient without new parcel taxes. During economic downturns, city revenues fall just as demand for essential services rises. Measure FF diversifies city revenue by making loan-to-own transactions, which continue during economic downturns, pay their fair share.
The measure rewards investments Oakland needs most. Buyers who convert distressed properties into affordable housing, shelter, or healthcare facilities receive a full refund. In other words, put a vacant building back to productive use and qualify for relief; hold it for speculation, and pay the same tax as everyone else.
Homeowners, small businesses, and working families pay this tax. Institutions best able to pay, like BlackRock, have been exempt. This measure ends that.

strong: Vote YES. Close the loophole. Improve city services.
